content: Tuberculosis (TB) infection is defined as a state in which an individual exhibits a persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) antigens, without any clinical evidence of active TB disease. It is estimated that approximately one-quarter of the global population is infected with Mtb. Identifying individuals with TB infection is critical, as it allows for targeted TB preventive treatment (TPT), which can significantly reduce the risk of progression to active TB disease. However, there is currently no gold-standard diagnostic test for TB infection. Two main classes of tests are available for diagnosing TB infection: the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). Both are indirect tests that rely on detecting immune sensitization to Mtb antigens. A positive result from either test does not reliably predict the likelihood of progression to active TB disease. The TST involves the intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD), a mixture of mycobacterial antigens, which elicits a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. The resulting induration at the injection site is measured 48–72 hours later. However, the TST is influenced by prior Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination and exposure to non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), which can lead to false-positive results. Additionally, the TST requires a follow-up visit for result interpretation, which can be logistically challenging. In contrast, IGRAs are in vitro blood tests that measure the release of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) by T-cells in response to stimulation with Mtb-specific antigens, such as early secretory antigenic target 6 (ESAT-6) and culture filtrate protein 10 (CFP-10). Unlike the TST, IGRAs are not affected by prior BCG vaccination or most NTM infections, making them more specific for Mtb infection. However, IGRAs are more expensive, require specialized laboratory facilities, and need trained personnel to perform the tests, limiting their accessibility in resource-limited settings. In 2011, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued recommendations on the use of IGRAs for diagnosing TB infection, including technologies such as the QuantiFERON®-TB Gold (QFT-G), QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT), and T-SPOT®.TB assays. In 2018, WHO updated its guidelines to recommend that either the TST or IGRAs (or both) could be used for TB infection testing, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The TST remains the most widely used test globally due to its lower cost and simpler implementation. More recently, newer TB antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) have been developed. These tests combine the simplicity of the TST with the specificity of IGRAs by using Mtb-specific antigens such as ESAT-6 and CFP-10. Emerging evidence suggests that TBSTs may have similar specificity to IGRAs and may provide more reliable results in children, adolescents, and people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, the evidence supporting these findings has not been systematically reviewed. In 2022, WHO issued recommendations on the use of TBSTs for diagnosing TB infection, including technologies such as Cy-Tb (Serum Institute of India), Diaskintest® (Generium, Russian Federation), and C-TST (formerly ESAT-6-CFP-10 test, Anhui Zhifei Longcom, China). The WHO guidelines aim to assess the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of TST, IGRAs, and TBSTs for TB infection, evaluate their concordance, and determine their impact on patient-important outcomes, such as the efficacy of TPT based on test results and the predictive value for progression to active TB disease. Additionally, the guidelines review qualitative data on feasibility, accessibility, equity, and end-user values, as well as economic data on affordability, cost, and cost-effectiveness. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) has emphasized that the diagnostic accuracy of TBSTs is comparable to that of IGRAs and superior to the TST. However, concerns remain regarding the quality of evidence, the lack of longitudinal studies assessing patient-important outcomes, and the potential for bias in non-blinded studies. The GDG strongly recommends the use of TST and IGRAs as equivalent options, with the choice of test depending on resource availability, infrastructure, and equity considerations. In resource-limited settings, the TST may be preferred due to its lower cost and greater familiarity among healthcare practitioners. However, the GDG has recommended against using IGRAs or TST as part of the diagnostic work-up for active TB in adults, including PLHIV, in LMICs, due to their low specificity and the risk of unnecessary treatment resulting from false-positive results. The current recommendations are based on evaluations of available data for all classes of TB infection diagnostic tests included in the respective assessments. Any new in-class technologies will require specific evaluation by WHO to determine their eligibility for procurement and use in TB diagnostics.
